q: Which is the best definition of a stakeholder?
options: Anyone who affects, or is affected by, the change
Only the people who fund the project
Only the end users of the system
Anyone who owns shares in the company
why: Stakeholders include anyone with a relationship to the change, need or solution, not just sponsors or users.

q: Halfway through a project, internal audit raises new control requirements nobody planned for. What most likely went wrong?
options: Audit was not identified as a stakeholder early
The sponsor approved the budget too early
The workshop had too many sticky notes
why: Missing a stakeholder early leads to late, unplanned requirements. Regulators and auditors belong on every stakeholder checklist.

q: The sponsor of an initiative is best described as the person who…
options: Authorizes and funds the work and makes final decisions
why: The sponsor authorizes the work, provides funding and resolves decisions beyond the team's authority.

q: Asking each stakeholder 'Who else should I talk to?' helps with…
options: Identifying stakeholders you might otherwise miss
why: This 'snowballing' approach uncovers additional stakeholders.

q: What does a stakeholder onion diagram show?
options: How far a change ripples, from the delivery team out to external parties
The order in which requirements will be built
why: The onion diagram places stakeholders in rings by their closeness to the solution.

q: A stakeholder has high power but low interest in your project. What is the recommended approach?
why: High power/low interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied: brief, targeted updates and consultation on key decisions.

q: Reconciliation analysts are deeply affected by the change but have little formal authority. Where do they sit on the power/interest grid?
why: Low power, high interest stakeholders should be kept informed and are often valuable SMEs.

q: In a RACI chart, how many people should be 'Accountable' for a single deliverable?
why: There should be only one Accountable person, so ownership is clear.

q: What is the difference between 'Consulted' and 'Informed' in RACI?
options: Consulted gives input before work is done; Informed is updated afterwards
Consulted signs off; Informed does the work
why: Consulted is two-way input before the work; Informed is one-way communication after decisions.

q: In RACI, the person who actually does the work is…
why: Responsible people perform the work; the Accountable person owns the outcome.

q: A powerful stakeholder is openly skeptical about the project. What is the best first step?
options: Meet one-on-one to understand their concerns and interests
Leave them off meeting invites to avoid conflict
Ask the sponsor to overrule them immediately
Send them the full requirements document and wait
why: Understanding a skeptic's interests early, one-on-one, is the best way to turn resistance into support.

q: Users say the documented procedure is followed, but you suspect workarounds. Which technique best reveals the real process?
why: Observation shows what people really do, including workarounds that may not appear in documents or interviews.

q: You need input from 300 branch staff across four countries in one week. Which technique fits best?
options: A single workshop with all 300 people
why: Surveys scale to large, distributed groups, although they don't allow follow-up questions.

q: Users struggle to describe the report layout they want but say 'I'll know it when I see it.' Which technique helps most?
why: Prototypes give users something concrete to react to.

q: What is a known risk of prototyping?
options: Users may believe the system is nearly finished
It only works for back-end systems
It eliminates the need for requirements
why: A realistic prototype can set false expectations about how close the solution is to completion.

q: Reviewing existing policies, procedure manuals and regulations to understand current rules is called…
why: Document analysis studies existing materials. Remember they may be out of date.

q: Prototypes, proofs of concept and A/B tests belong to which category of elicitation?
why: BABOK groups elicitation into collaborative, research and experiments. Prototypes and A/B tests are experiments.

q: What defines a structured interview?
options: A prepared set of questions asked in a fixed order
An informal chat with no plan
A group session with sticky notes
why: Structured interviews use predefined questions in order, so answers can be compared across interviewees.

q: Which is an open question?
options: Walk me through what happens when a payment fails to match.
Do you check the report daily?
Have you used the new screen?
why: Open questions invite explanation. The others can be answered with yes/no or a single fact.

q: Why should a BA avoid the question 'You'd prefer automatic matching, right?'
options: It is a leading question that biases the answer
why: Leading questions suggest the answer and undermine impartial fact-finding.

q: After an interview, what should the BA do to confirm the results?
options: Send a summary back to the interviewee to check accuracy
Send notes straight to developers as final requirements
Delete the notes once the meeting ends
Wait until the end of the project to review them
why: Confirming elicitation results with the source ensures accuracy before the information is used.

q: Paraphrasing what an interviewee said ('So if I understand correctly…') is an example of…
why: Active listening includes paraphrasing and summarizing to confirm understanding.

q: Which closing question helps uncover missed information in an interview?
options: Is there anything I should have asked but didn't?
Do you agree with my solution?
why: This open closing question often surfaces important issues the BA didn't think to ask about.

q: In a requirements workshop, what is the purpose of a 'parking lot'?
options: To capture off-topic items so the session stays focused
why: A parking lot records valuable but off-topic issues for later, keeping the agenda on track.

q: What should a workshop facilitator do to stay effective?
options: Remain neutral and guide the process, not push their own solution
Make all decisions for the group
Let the most senior person speak the whole time
Skip the agenda to stay flexible
why: The facilitator manages the process neutrally so the group reaches its own decisions.

q: One participant dominates a workshop and others stay silent. What is a good technique?
options: Use round-robin or silent brainstorming so everyone contributes
Ask the dominant person to leave
why: Structured turn-taking or silent idea generation balances participation.

q: A workshop should end with…
options: A summary of decisions, open issues and action items with owners and dates
A request for everyone to email their notes later
A vote on the project budget
why: Closing with decisions and owned, dated actions turns discussion into progress.

q: Who records decisions and requirements during a workshop?
why: The scribe captures outputs so the facilitator can focus on running the session.

q: A stakeholder keeps sending new feature requests that aren't linked to any project objective. What should the BA do?
options: Trace each request to an objective and route new items through change control
Add every request to scope to keep them happy
why: Linking requests to objectives and using change control manages scope creep.

q: An expert says 'we just know which breaks to ignore' but can't explain the rule. Which technique helps capture this tacit knowledge?
why: Tacit knowledge is hard to verbalize; observing the work and asking about each decision reveals it.
